title: Helix Health - Private installer upgrade blocker triage (stuck at migrations)
next_steps: Helix to run Redwood installer diagnostics collection steps (installer logs + cluster events) and upload bundle to the existing secure ticket thread (SUP-1845).
Redwood (Ethan/Benji) to review migration job logs and advise whether the safe rollback procedure is recommended vs a forward-fix (manual unlock / rerun).
Support (Dev) to update SUP-1845 with the agreed customer-facing guidance and link the draft KB article for upgrade stuck at migrations once published.
Redwood to confirm whether any known issue exists for this installer version + their cluster distro and add notes to the workaround article (temporary) if validated.

Helix (Maya): Export Kubernetes events from `redwood-system` and `redwood-control-plane` namespaces for the last 2 hours around the attempt. Due: 2026-02-06
Helix (Maya): Capture status of migration job/pod (name, restart count) and any CrashLoop logs. Due: 2026-02-06
Redwood (Ethan): Provide exact rollback command sequence + validation checklist (API health + console login + audit logs). Due: 2026-02-06
Redwood (Benji): Confirm whether migration lock table is safe to inspect/clear and what evidence we need before recommending it. Due: 2026-02-06

summary: Helix Health reported a blocked Redwood Private upgrade where the installer progresses but hangs/fails at the database migrations step. Redwood and Helix walked through what “stuck at migrations” typically means (migrations job pending/crashlooping, database connectivity, schema lock, or resource constraints), aligned on a safe diagnostics bundle to collect, and agreed on a conservative rollback plan if forward-fix cannot be validated quickly. The conversation stayed focused on minimizing risk for a compliance-heavy environment and keeping Support/Engineering escalation paths clean (SUP-1845).
topics: Symptoms + timeline of the failed Private upgrade (installer stage: migrations)
What diagnostics to collect safely (installer logs, k8s events, job logs, DB connectivity checks)
Likely failure modes (lock contention, permissions, disk pressure, image pull, network policy)
Rollback decision criteria and step-by-step validation
Escalation and communications plan tied to SUP-1845
transcript:
Meeting: Helix Health - Private installer upgrade blocker triage (stuck at migrations)
Date: 2026-02-06
Time: 16:03 UTC
Duration: 51 min

Attendees (Redwood): Rachel Kim, Dev Patel, Ethan Park, Benji Okafor, Sean Gallagher
Attendees (Helix Health): Maya Desai, Tom Reynolds, Anika Rao, Javier Ortega

---

[00:00] Rachel Kim: Alright, I think we’re live. Thanks everyone for jumping on short notice. This is the Helix Private upgrade blocker triage—specifically the installer upgrade getting stuck at migrations. We’re anchored on SUP-1845, so we’ll keep notes there. Maya, Tom, do you want to give us the quick recap and what “stuck” looks like on your side?

[00:22] Maya Desai: Yeah. So we were upgrading our Private control plane from the previous bundle to the new one that Support shared. The installer runs, pulls images, and then it gets to the migrations step—like it says “running migrations,” and then it just… doesn’t complete. We let it go for, I don’t know, 40 minutes. Then we stopped it, retried, and the second time it actually failed with like a timeout.

[00:51] Tom Reynolds: And we saw one of the pods, I think it was the migration job, was restarting. We didn’t want to poke too much because we’re trying to stay within your supported path.

[01:04] Dev Patel: That’s perfect, thank you. And for context, this is still non-prod or is it your prod cluster?

[01:10] Maya Desai: This is our staging cluster, but it’s staging that mirrors prod pretty tightly. Same network policies, same database engine, all that.

[01:18] Rachel Kim: Got it. And impact right now is upgrade blocked but no outage in staging other than you can’t complete the upgrade. Correct?

[01:24] Maya Desai: Correct. Current version is functioning.

[01:27] Anika Rao: From compliance side, we’re also cautious about any manual DB changes. Just flagging that upfront.

[01:33] Ethan Park: Totally. We’ll avoid anything “ad-hoc” unless we’re very explicit and it’s reversible. Let me ask: when you say timeout, is it the installer reporting “migration step exceeded” or is it the job itself failing?

[01:47] Maya Desai: The installer printed something like “waiting for migrations to complete” and then eventually “context deadline exceeded.” I can paste the exact line in the ticket.

[01:57] Benji Okafor: If you have the installer log from that run, that’s the main artifact. There’s usually a section that tells us which k8s job it’s waiting on.

[02:06] Sean Gallagher: And just to set expectations: migrations can take a while if there’s lock contention or if the DB is under-provisioned, but 40 minutes for a typical control plane schema change is… on the high side.

[02:20] Tom Reynolds: Yeah, agreed. In staging we’re using smaller DB instance size, but it’s not tiny.

[02:26] Ethan Park: Okay. Let’s do this systematically. I want three buckets of data: (1) installer logs, (2) Kubernetes events + job/pod logs for the migrations job, (3) any DB connectivity errors or resource pressure in the namespace.

[02:41] Dev Patel: And to be clear, we don’t need secrets. Please redact tokens, endpoints if needed, but timestamps and error strings are good.

[02:49] Maya Desai: Yep.

[02:50] Rachel Kim: Before we jump into collection, I want to confirm the exact package/version you’re upgrading to. I think Support attached the 1.18.2 private bundle—does that match?

[03:00] Maya Desai: Yes, the private installer bundle is 1.18.2. The runtime piece in it is 1.18.0 something, I don’t know if that’s relevant.

[03:08] Ethan Park: It can be, but for the installer stuck at migrations, it’s usually control plane DB. Benji, do we have a known issue around 1.18.2 migrations on certain Postgres versions?

[03:18] Benji Okafor: Not that I’m aware of. There is a change that adds an index for audit log stuff—sorry, “audit log” might be the wrong term, but it touches the pipeline tables. If their DB is on an older minor version, sometimes it behaves differently. We need the DB version too.

[03:36] Tom Reynolds: We’re on Postgres 14.8.

[03:39] Benji Okafor: That should be fine.

[03:42] Sean Gallagher: Another thing is if there’s a network policy preventing the job from hitting the DB—then it loops.

[03:49] Maya Desai: We do have strict network policies. But it worked in the previous version.

[03:55] Ethan Park: Sure, but if we changed the job’s labels or service account or it runs in a different namespace, policy might not match. That’s why events are useful.

[04:05] Rachel Kim: Maya, can you describe what you saw in Kubernetes? You mentioned restarts.

[04:10] Maya Desai: We saw a job pod, name had “migrate” in it. It was in CrashLoopBackOff. We did a quick “kubectl logs” and it said something like “could not acquire lock” or “waiting for lock.” Again, I need to pull the exact lines.

[04:26] Ethan Park: That’s a key detail. If it’s a migration lock, we need to check whether another migration attempt left a lock row or a transaction open. But we should not jump to “clear locks” without seeing evidence.

[04:39] Anika Rao: +1. No manual DB changes unless we have a supported path.

[04:44] Dev Patel: For the ticket, we can frame it as diagnostics first. If we can do a forward-fix by rerunning migrations after a clean stop, that’s preferable.

[04:54] Sean Gallagher: Also, if you ran the installer twice, it might have left two jobs. Sometimes the installer will create a new job name each run, and the old one is still around. That can confuse “waiting” behavior.

[05:08] Tom Reynolds: That’s possible. We didn’t delete anything.

[05:11] Benji Okafor: Great, then one of the first commands is just: list jobs in the namespace and see duplicates.

[05:18] Ethan Park: Exactly. Okay, I’m going to outline the minimal collection steps. Maya or Tom, you can run these whenever and paste results in SUP-1845.

[05:27] Ethan Park: Step 1: Installer logs. Wherever you ran the installer from, grab `installer.log` plus any debug log—sometimes it’s `installer-debug.log`. We need the entire block around the migrations stage.

[05:41] Ethan Park: Step 2: Kubernetes events. For namespaces `redwood-system` and `redwood-control-plane`—export events for the last couple hours: `kubectl get events -n ... --sort-by=.lastTimestamp`.

[05:55] Ethan Park: Step 3: Identify the migration job/pod. `kubectl get jobs -n redwood-control-plane | grep -i mig` and `kubectl get pods -n redwood-control-plane | grep -i mig`. Then `kubectl describe pod <pod>` and `kubectl logs <pod> --previous` if it’s restarting.

[06:12] Tom Reynolds: Okay.

[06:13] Ethan Park: Step 4: Resource pressure check. `kubectl describe node` is too broad, but at least `kubectl top pods -n redwood-control-plane` if metrics-server is installed, and `kubectl get pods -n ...` to see pending states.

[06:27] Maya Desai: We have metrics-server, yes.

[06:30] Benji Okafor: Also image pull errors show up as events. We’ve seen cases where it’s not actually migrations, it’s image pull backoff and the installer is just “waiting.”

[06:40] Sean Gallagher: Right. And if you can capture the exact pod exit code, that helps. Like `exit 137` vs `exit 1`.

[06:48] Rachel Kim: And all of this stays within the Support ticket, not pasted into a broad doc. Just reiterating.

[06:54] Javier Ortega: Thanks. For our side, that’s fine.

[06:57] Dev Patel: While we’re on it, I want to ask about rollback appetite. If we determine it’s not safe to proceed quickly, do you want to roll back the attempted upgrade? Or since staging is okay, you can hold?

[07:10] Tom Reynolds: We can hold in staging. But we want a rollback plan documented before we try again, because we can’t afford to break prod later.

[07:18] Maya Desai: Agree.

[07:19] Ethan Park: Makes sense. Let’s talk rollback in a conservative way. First principle: we only roll back if the installer changed deployed components and the old version isn’t stable. Since you said current version is functioning, we might not need rollback right now. But we should prepare.

[07:37] Sean Gallagher: “Rollback” here can mean two things: rolling back Kubernetes workloads (Helm release) vs rolling back DB schema. DB rollback is riskier.

[07:46] Anika Rao: DB rollback is the one that makes us nervous.

[07:49] Ethan Park: Same. Our standard supported rollback is: stop the upgrade, ensure no migration job is running, redeploy the previous control plane manifests, and confirm API health. We generally do not do “down migrations” unless we have a tested path.

[08:08] Benji Okafor: In practice, if migrations partially applied, the older control plane is typically forward-compatible for a short window, but it depends. That’s why the migration logs matter.

[08:20] Rachel Kim: Ethan, can we give them a checklist, like “if you see X, do Y”?

[08:24] Ethan Park: Yes. The decision tree is:
- If migrations haven’t applied any changes (job never ran / couldn’t connect), rollback is safe by redeploying previous release.
- If migrations started and applied some steps, we need to confirm compatibility before redeploying old version.

[08:43] Tom Reynolds: How do we tell if migrations applied steps without manual DB inspection?

[08:49] Ethan Park: Good question. Usually the migration tool logs each step. The log indicates whether it’s executing step N, or “already applied.” If we have that, we can infer state without you querying the DB.

[09:04] Benji Okafor: There’s also sometimes a “schema version” table. But again, that’s DB inspection.

[09:09] Anika Rao: We can do read-only queries, but we’d prefer to avoid any writes.

[09:14] Sean Gallagher: Read-only is generally fine. If needed, we can provide a single SELECT that’s safe. But let’s see logs first.

[09:24] Dev Patel: For Support workflow, we’ll keep it as “collect logs first; do not clear locks or edit DB without Redwood instruction.”

[09:33] Maya Desai: Sounds good.

[09:35] Rachel Kim: Can you also describe your installer execution environment? Like, where did you run it from? Bastion? CI?

[09:42] Tom Reynolds: From a bastion host in the same VPC. It has kubectl access and access to the private container registry.

[09:49] Benji Okafor: And it uses the same kubeconfig as your admin user?

[09:52] Tom Reynolds: Yes.

[09:53] Ethan Park: Okay. Another frequent cause: the service account used by the job doesn’t have permissions if RBAC changed. Then the job fails early. Again, events show that.

[10:06] Maya Desai: Our RBAC is fairly standard but we do have some policies.

[10:10] Sean Gallagher: One more thing: disk pressure on the DB volume can cause migrations to hang, especially if it’s adding indexes. Not common, but possible.

[10:19] Tom Reynolds: DB volume has enough free space, but we can confirm.

[10:24] Rachel Kim: Just to align on comms: Dev, do we want to set expectation of update cadence? This is staging but it’s a blocker.

[10:31] Dev Patel: Yep. For a Private blocker with no outage, we’ll treat it as P2 unless they say prod is impacted. We can commit to same-business-day updates, and if we identify risk to prod timeline, we’ll escalate to SRE/Platform on-call. Since Ethan and Benji are already here, we’re good.

[10:50] Javier Ortega: That works.

[10:52] Rachel Kim: Okay.

[10:54] Ethan Park: Let’s dig into what “lock” could mean. Maya said the log might have “could not acquire lock.” That suggests the migration framework uses an advisory lock. If a previous attempt crashed while holding it, it should release, because advisory locks are tied to the DB session. Unless there’s a row-based lock or a “lock table” row.

[11:18] Benji Okafor: In our code path, it’s a “migrations_lock” table entry. If the process dies at the wrong time, it can leave a row that prevents subsequent runs. But we have a TTL in newer versions. Not sure if 1.18.2 includes the TTL; I think it does.

[11:35] Sean Gallagher: If it’s leaving a lock row, we need to understand why, because that would be a product bug.

[11:42] Ethan Park: Agreed.

[11:44] Maya Desai: Sorry, can I clarify? The error might have been “another migration is running.” Something like that.

[11:49] Ethan Park: That’s consistent.

[11:51] Tom Reynolds: We also saw the job starting, then restarting.

[11:56] Benji Okafor: Restart could be OOMKilled, which would leave lock state depending on when it wrote it.

[12:03] Sean Gallagher: OOMKilled could happen if it loads a large table, but again, we need the exit code.

[12:10] Rachel Kim: This is great. So, data points needed: OOM vs permissions vs network.

[12:16] Dev Patel: Can we add a quick “kubectl get pod -o jsonpath” command? That’s sometimes too much. Maybe “kubectl describe” is enough.

[12:24] Ethan Park: Describe is enough.

[12:26] Anika Rao: On logs, just confirming: please don’t ask us to share anything that includes PHI. Our staging is de-identified but still.

[12:33] Rachel Kim: Understood. We do not need payload data. Just system logs.

[12:37] Ethan Park: The migration logs should not include customer data. If you see any tables or IDs that look sensitive, feel free to redact them.

[12:46] Maya Desai: Okay.

[12:48] Rachel Kim: Switching gears: do you have a deadline for this upgrade? Any external go-live?

[12:53] Javier Ortega: We’re trying to align with an internal release end of month. But prod upgrade would be later; this is our early validation.

[13:02] Rachel Kim: Got it.

[13:04] Dev Patel: For SUP-1845 we’ll note “not prod, but blocks validation; target resolution this week.”

[13:12] Sean Gallagher: Ethan, do we have a newer installer build with better diagnostics? I recall ENG-4828 is in flight.

[13:18] Ethan Park: Yes, there’s an engineering task to add a diagnostics bundle and clearer output. Not shipped yet. For now, we can give manual steps.

[13:27] Benji Okafor: We can also run the installer with a verbose flag. But I don’t remember if it’s `--debug` or `--verbose`.

[13:34] Tom Reynolds: I think we ran `--debug` on the second attempt.

[13:38] Benji Okafor: Great, then `installer-debug.log` should exist.

[13:43] Rachel Kim: Perfect.

[13:45] Ethan Park: When you re-run, do not keep re-running repeatedly. Each attempt can create more jobs and confuse state. Let’s first collect artifacts from the last run.

[13:58] Maya Desai: Understood.

[14:00] Rachel Kim: Can we talk about a “safe stop” procedure? Like if the installer is hanging, what is the safe way to stop it without leaving things half-done?

[14:10] Ethan Park: Safe stop: Ctrl-C is okay, but then confirm no migration job is still running. If it is, we need to decide whether to let it finish or delete the job. Deleting the job is generally safe, but we should confirm it’s not in the middle of applying a step. That’s why we prefer to check logs.

[14:30] Sean Gallagher: If the job is CrashLooping, it’s not making progress anyway.

[14:34] Tom Reynolds: Makes sense.

[14:36] Dev Patel: For Support doc, we’ll phrase it: “Stop installer, capture logs, do not delete pods/jobs unless Redwood instructs.”

[14:45] Rachel Kim: Good.

[14:47] Ethan Park: Let’s simulate what we’ll do once we have logs. Scenario A: network policy blocks DB access. Then fix is adjusting policy to allow the migration job’s labels/service account to connect. Scenario B: OOMKilled. Fix is temporary resource bump for job. Scenario C: lock row. Fix might be a supported script to clear the lock after verifying no other migration is running.

[15:14] Anika Rao: For scenario C, would you provide a script we run, or is it something you can do remotely?

[15:20] Ethan Park: In Private, we cannot access your DB. We’d provide a command, you run it.

[15:26] Anika Rao: Okay.

[15:28] Rachel Kim: We’ll keep that inside the ticket thread.

[15:31] Benji Okafor: Also, there’s a scenario D: the migration tool is waiting on a “leader election” config map and can’t write it due to RBAC. That can look like a hang. Logs will show “forbidden” errors.

[15:47] Maya Desai: Yeah, we do use restrictive RBAC for some namespaces.

[15:51] Tom Reynolds: But our admin user can create jobs and pods.

[15:55] Benji Okafor: It’s not the admin user; it’s the service account inside the job.

[15:59] Tom Reynolds: Right.

[16:01] Rachel Kim: Good catch.

[16:03] Dev Patel: Quick admin question: are you okay if we invite Naomi Feldman from security if we need to touch anything policy-related? Or keep it limited?

[16:12] Anika Rao: We can loop security later if needed. For now, this group is fine.

[16:18] Rachel Kim: Great.

[16:20] Ethan Park: Maya, can you recall the namespace where the migration job ran? You said control plane.

[16:24] Maya Desai: It was `redwood-control-plane`, yes.

[16:27] Ethan Park: Good.

[16:28] Sean Gallagher: In some older installs, it’s `redwood-platform`. But okay.

[16:33] Maya Desai: Ours is `redwood-control-plane`.

[16:35] Benji Okafor: Cool.

[16:36] Rachel Kim: Since we’re waiting on data, can we discuss “rollback plan” in more concrete steps? Tom asked for it.

[16:43] Ethan Park: Sure. High-level rollback plan (supported):
1) Confirm current prod/staging health before change (API returns 200, console login works).
2) If upgrade attempt fails, stop installer.
3) Confirm migrations job is not running / no pods in Running state for migrations.
4) Redeploy previous release artifacts (previous installer bundle) to restore workloads.
5) Validate: control plane API health endpoint, auth/SSO if configured, audit log pipeline if enabled, and any critical integrations.
6) Monitor logs for 30-60 minutes.

[17:18] Ethan Park: What we don’t recommend as default: running “down migrations.” If schema changed forward, old version might still operate; if it doesn’t, we need an engineering-guided plan.

[17:34] Tom Reynolds: And step 4 is basically running the old installer bundle again?

[17:39] Ethan Park: Yes, with the appropriate “apply” mode. It should reconcile back to the previous images/manifests.

[17:47] Benji Okafor: Make sure you keep the same config values file.

[17:50] Maya Desai: Okay.

[17:51] Anika Rao: In that plan, do we need to snapshot the database before upgrade?

[17:56] Sean Gallagher: For compliance-heavy customers, yes, we strongly recommend a DB snapshot before any control plane upgrade. It’s your standard practice anyway.

[18:06] Tom Reynolds: We do snapshots.

[18:08] Rachel Kim: We can include “recommended pre-req: snapshot” in the ticket.

[18:12] Dev Patel: I’ll add it in SUP-1845 as a note.

[18:15] Ethan Park: Another rollback validation: check your agent connectivity from data plane to control plane, if you’re running separate clusters. Do you have that separation?

[18:26] Maya Desai: Yes, data plane is separate, but in staging we run them together sometimes. It’s complicated.

[18:33] Ethan Park: No worries. Just note what you’re using for this environment. Again, the installer logs might have cluster topology.

[18:42] Rachel Kim: Okay.

[18:44] Tom Reynolds: One question: should we delete the failed migration job before re-running the installer? Or let it sit?

[18:51] Ethan Park: Don’t delete yet. List jobs first. If there are multiple and none are running, we can decide. In many cases, leaving it is fine; the new run creates a new job. But if the installer is waiting on the “latest” job name, older jobs won’t matter.

[19:10] Benji Okafor: Sometimes it waits on a label selector, like `app=migrations`. Then multiple jobs can confuse it.

[19:18] Ethan Park: Exactly. Logs will say.

[19:21] Sean Gallagher: If you do see multiple jobs, grab their statuses: completions, duration, last condition.

[19:28] Maya Desai: Got it.

[19:30] Rachel Kim: Let’s also align on escalation if this becomes prod-impacting. Dev, what’s the threshold?

[19:36] Dev Patel: If they attempt prod upgrade and control plane is degraded—auth failures, API unavailable—then it’s P0/P1, immediate SRE + Platform page and bridge per playbook. For now, staging blocker is P2.

[19:50] Javier Ortega: Okay.

[19:52] Rachel Kim: Thanks.

[19:54] Ethan Park: Can you share whether you’re using external Postgres or in-cluster?

[19:59] Tom Reynolds: External managed Postgres.

[20:02] Ethan Park: Great. That reduces some variables.

[20:05] Benji Okafor: Are there any proxies in between? Like a sidecar or a DB proxy.

[20:09] Tom Reynolds: We use a standard internal load balancer, not a proxy. No pgbouncer.

[20:15] Benji Okafor: Okay.

[20:16] Sean Gallagher: If there’s no pgbouncer, advisory lock behavior is straightforward.

[20:21] Maya Desai: We do have mTLS between namespaces. Could that matter?

[20:26] Ethan Park: If the migration job uses the same client library and certs as the API pods, it should be fine. But if it’s a different image or missing cert mounts, it could fail to connect.

[20:40] Tom Reynolds: That’s possible.

[20:42] Benji Okafor: Then logs would show TLS handshake failure.

[20:45] Rachel Kim: Great.

[20:47] Dev Patel: Just to ensure we’re not missing something: can you paste the “installer version” output? Like `installer --version`.

[20:55] Maya Desai: Yes.

[20:56] Dev Patel: Add that to the ticket too.

[20:59] Rachel Kim: Okay.

[21:01] (cross talk)

[21:02] Rachel Kim: Sorry, go ahead Tom.

[21:04] Tom Reynolds: If we need to run a single read-only query for schema version, are you comfortable providing that?

[21:10] Ethan Park: Yes. But let’s wait. If we do, it’ll be like `SELECT version FROM schema_migrations ORDER BY applied_at DESC LIMIT 5;` or similar. We’ll tailor it once we confirm the table name in your deployment.

[21:25] Anika Rao: As long as it’s read-only, okay.

[21:28] Sean Gallagher: And we’ll ask you to run it in a controlled window.

[21:33] Rachel Kim: Great.

[21:35] Dev Patel: While we have everyone: we’re also drafting a known-issues article for “Private installer upgrade stuck at migrations.” Once we confirm root cause and workaround, we’ll publish a customer-safe version. We’ll keep any Helix specifics out.

[21:50] Maya Desai: That’s helpful.

[21:52] Ethan Park: Cool. Another check: what Kubernetes version are you on?

[21:56] Maya Desai: 1.27.

[21:58] Benji Okafor: Supported.

[22:00] Sean Gallagher: Yep.

[22:02] Rachel Kim: Okay. Anything else you want to cover while we wait on logs? Maybe timeline? When can you share artifacts?

[22:10] Tom Reynolds: We can do it right after this call. Give us 30 minutes.

[22:14] Dev Patel: Great. I’ll stay on the ticket and respond as soon as it’s in.

[22:18] Ethan Park: If you can, also include the output of `kubectl version` and `kubectl get ns | grep redwood` just to confirm names.

[22:27] Maya Desai: Sure.

[22:29] Rachel Kim: Thanks.

[22:31] Ethan Park: Let’s talk about “if we need to rerun.” Once we review, we might ask you to:
- Delete only the migrations job (not DB)
- Re-run installer with `--debug`
- Or temporarily bump resources for that job

[22:46] Ethan Park: But we won’t do that until we see evidence.

[22:50] Anika Rao: Appreciate the caution.

[22:52] Sean Gallagher: Also: please don’t change network policies in an ad-hoc way. If we suspect that, we’ll identify the exact rule needed.

[23:02] Tom Reynolds: Understood.

[23:04] Rachel Kim: One more thing: does this upgrade include any change to SSO or identity components? We had a separate SSO ticket in the queue, but not for Helix.

[23:13] Maya Desai: Not that we’re aware. We use SAML, but it’s stable.

[23:17] Ethan Park: Migrations shouldn’t touch SSO.

[23:20] Benji Okafor: Unless there’s a new column for audit logs. Sorry, I keep saying audit logs—it might be “event logs.”

[23:27] Dev Patel: It’s fine.

[23:28] Rachel Kim: Okay.

[23:30] Ethan Park: To wrap: artifacts to send: installer log, debug log, k8s events, job/pod logs, describe output, and maybe a note about DB size/resources. That’s enough.

[23:44] Maya Desai: Got it.

[23:45] Rachel Kim: We’ll pause here. But before we end, I want to confirm: if the upgrade is stuck and we need to roll back, we’re not recommending any DB down-migration. Just redeploy previous workloads and verify. Correct?

[23:58] Ethan Park: Correct.

[23:59] Sean Gallagher: Correct.

[24:01] Tom Reynolds: Okay.

[24:02] Rachel Kim: Great.

[24:04] (Later in call - continued discussion after log review; notes reflect live screen share)

[24:06] Dev Patel: Maya just pasted a snippet in chat. I’m reading: “migration lock already held, exiting” and then it restarts.

[24:15] Ethan Park: Okay, that’s useful. It says “lock already held.” That means the job thinks another migration is running, or a lock record exists.

[24:25] Benji Okafor: Does it say anything about the lock owner? Sometimes it prints a UUID.

[24:29] Maya Desai: It prints something like “lock id: 9f… something.” I’ll paste full line in ticket.

[24:37] Sean Gallagher: If it’s a stale lock record, the “supported” way is to verify no other migration pods are running, then clear lock record.

[24:46] Anika Rao: That’s a write, right?

[24:48] Ethan Park: Yes, it is a write. So we need to be careful: confirm no active migrations, then do a targeted delete of the lock row. We will provide the exact statement.

[25:00] Rachel Kim: Are we comfortable recommending that for staging only, while we work on a permanent fix?

[25:06] Ethan Park: For staging, yes, with caution. For prod, we’d likely want to patch the installer or the migration tool to handle stale lock TTL.
